results.fact: Route grade vs crux pitch grade
results.evidence: The published pitch-by-pitch breakdown lists P2 5.11b and P4/P5 5.11+ with an overall grade of plain 5.11; a second detailed report lists the same pitch grades (5.11+ on P4 and P5) yet gives the whole route as 5.11b. One source notes the P4 crux can be aided to bring it to 5.10. The sources themselves pair a 5.11b headline with 5.11+ pitches, and no two agree on a different overall letter grade, so there is no researched value to adopt.

results.fact: Crux difficulty (5.0 vs a reported 5.4 move)

results.evidence: The route database page grades the West Ridge Easy 5th and calls the crux slabby depression 'Class 4/5'; it never mentions 5.4. An independent trip report rates the ridge Class 4. The '5.4' appears to come from a club listing that asks participants to be comfortable leading 5.4 single-pitch trad, a prerequisite rather than the route's grade.

results.correct_value: Jul-Sep has less snow and rockfall, but water on the ridge gets scarcer as the season goes on
results.evidence: The route's own season, pro_tips and watch_out all say water becomes the crux late in the season. The route's published description agrees: early season has more snow and rockfall risk, late season less overhead hazard but water becomes scarce, and water plus conditions are the cruxes. best_season's 'for water availability' reverses this.

patches.find: for water availability and less snow.

results.fact: Commitment grade IV vs 'Grade III' quoted in the approach text
results.evidence: The approach sentence explicitly labels 'Grade III, 5.6-5.7' as the grade of the standard North Face Route on North Peak (the first section of the traverse), not of the traverse; the traverse's own IV is a separate, clearly labelled route fact. Published grades for that North Face route range from III to IV, so the sentence is not wrong about the sub-route.

results.evidence: The Forest Service lists the Lake Serene Trail and trailhead as a Skykomish Ranger District site of Mt. results.fact: Total gain 4,500 ft is less than the trailhead-to-summit rise
results.evidence: gain_ft is 4,500, but the route starts at the ~600 ft trailhead and ends on Main Peak (high_point_ft 5,991), a net rise of ~5,400 ft before counting the ups and downs between the three summits; the sibling Main Peak route stores 5,800 ft. No published total-gain figure for the full traverse was found, so no value was adopted.

dist_km is the one-way approach distance and the itinerary miles are per day across a round trip, so 3.6 mi one-way vs 9.5-10 mi round trip compare different quantities. Published one-way lengths for the Lake Serene trail itself differ (3.5 mi from the Forest Service, 4.1 mi from the trail guide), so 3.6 mi sits within the range of the trail distance and no single one-way figure is established to replace it.

results.fact: Pitch count on the North Face section
results.evidence: The North Face of North Peak is listed as 12 pitches (1,400 ft, 5.7). A detailed ascent account logged about 11 roped pitches from 3rd class to 5.7 after two pitches of scrambling. Both agree with the itinerary's '~12 pitches'; the 4 comes from a placeholder count on the traverse listing, and the 4-row ROUTE BREAKDOWN is a list of sections, not pitches.

results.fact: Turnaround plan vs. the route's own multi-day schedule
results.correct_value: A turnaround tied to the North Face on the climbing day, not a single-day 5-hour / 2 PM rule
results.evidence: timing (29 hrs) and all three itinerary days describe a 3-day trip that tops out North Peak around noon on day 2 and bivies on the ridge. External accounts agree it is a long multi-day effort: the first traverse party reached North Peak by noon and spent a night on the ridge, and a recent party spent 10 hours on the North Face and got only halfway. The 'after 5 hours / by 2 PM' turnaround is copied from a short day route.

patches.fact: Turnaround plan vs. the route's own multi-day schedule
patches.expect: Turn around by 2 PM if still climbing after 5 hours; summit will not be reached by safe descent time.
patches.value: This is a multi-day climb, so plan around the bivies rather than a single-day clock. The real decision point is the North Face on the climbing day: if you have not topped out on North Peak by mid-afternoon, rappel the face then, because once past North Peak retreating is usually harder than continuing.

results.fact: Descent line: reverse the North Face vs descend the East Route/Hourglass Gully
results.evidence: descent and descent_text say parties finishing on Main Peak descend the East Route/Hourglass Gully to Lake Serene and should not reverse the ascent line, but itinerary day 3 (title, note, objective, schedule), timing.sectionBreakdown[2] and itinerary.totalNote say the party reverses the North Face by rappel back to the NE spur. A logged traverse describes descending the East Route to Lake Serene with one short rappel and brush belays, and the East Route/Hourglass Gully is Main Peak's standard line; a second independent traverse account confirming the descent could not be read (pages blocked), so no rewrite was made.

results.fact: Season window for a route named '(Winter)'
results.evidence: The route listing presents it as the way to reach Main Peak in winter. One party climbed it on May 21 and advises against going any later than May because snow cover is what makes the forested ridge passable, the gully melting out to 5th-class rock in summer; another climbed it in January on hard snow and blue ice. That matches best_season, beta and approach_variants (winter through May, best Mar-Apr), not a Late Apr-Oct scramble window.

patches.fact: Season window for a route named '(Winter)'
patches.expect: Late Apr-Oct for the general scramble; best as a snow climb roughly May-Jun when the gully's crux rock step is still snow-bridged; not recommended in mid-late summer (bare wet rock, brutal bushwhacking) or unstable winter conditions

results.evidence: gear, rack, detailed_rack, descent and rappel_detail all say two 30 m ropes. A party that climbed it brought two 30 m ropes and made two or three rappels; a winter party carrying only a single 30 m rope reported being forced into dangerous downclimbing. rope_length_m 60 / 'single' is the outlier.

results.fact: Timing component hours don't sum to totalHrs
results.evidence: The row's itinerary gives 2-3 hrs to the lake plus 2-3 hrs to the saddle (about 5 hrs car to saddle), 2-3 hrs up the gully plus 1-2 on the ridge, and 2-3 hrs each for the rappels, the return to the lake and the hike-out; the turnaround text budgets 8-10 hrs up and 4-6 down. Parties report about 12 hours car to car, and a 2:30 AM start still out after sunset; approach_variants says 12-15 hrs is normal. So the 15-hour total stands and the approach and descent components were understated.

results.fact: Total gain/loss: gain_ft 6,000 vs loss_ft 5,500 vs approach '~5,500 ft' on an out-and-back
results.evidence: The route goes up and back the same way ('Descend via the same route'), yet gain_ft is 6,000, loss_ft 5,500, the approach text says ~5,500 ft of gain and approach_variants 'over 6,000 ft'.
